https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/ww3-fears.text: Ethan Davies Updated Thu, September 24, 2026 at 5:34 AM UTC 0 A Russian Mi-8 helicopter entered Polish airspace on Wednesday morning (Image: Getty) NATO air defences were activated for the third time in two days, as fears of an all-out war between Russia and the West have soared. Russia conducted massive drone strikes on eastern Ukraine on Thursday morning (September 24), prompting Poland to activate its ground-based air defences in response . Poland also said strikes in Ukraine 24 hours earlier required air defences to be launched, and the country's air force scrambled fighter jets when a Russian helicopter 'violated' Polish airspace later on Wednesday morning. Poland's Operational Command of the Armed Forces said in a statement, posted at 5:22am UK time: "In connection with the strikes by the Russian Federation on the territory of Ukraine, conducted using air attack assets, military aviation is operating in Polish airspace. "In accordance with applicable procedures, the Operational Command of the Armed Forces RSZ, through the Air Operations Centre - Air Component Command, has activated the necessary forces and resources at its disposal. Ground-based air defence systems and radar reconnaissance systems have reached readiness status. "These actions are of a preventive nature and are aimed at securing airspace and its protection, especially in areas adjacent to threatened regions. The Operational Command of the Armed Forces RSZ is monitoring the current situation, and subordinate forces and resources remain ready for immediate response." It posted a similar message when it activated the same defences around 24 hours earlier, triggered when Russian drones killed at least nine people in massive strikes across Kyiv and Dnipro. In the hours after the strikes, Poland accused Russia of entering its airspace without permission. Military commanders said a Russian Mi-8 chopper 'briefly violated' the airspace near the town of Braniewo, close to Russia's Kaliningrad exclave on the Baltic Sea. It strayed into Poland's airspace by 300m for 42 seconds at 11:08am local time. Commanders confirmed jets were scrambled. They said: "The flight of the machine was observed by the radio-location systems of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Poland. Fighter aircraft were scrambled, and ground-based forces and assets remained on standby. "The nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defence. The crews of the Republic of Poland's air defence systems conduct round-the-clock observation, remaining in constant readiness to ensure the safety of Polish airspace." Around the same time, there were unconfirmed reports from Romania that a unidentified drone entered its airspace. Reportedly, the country's air operations services spotted the drone flying through the airspace at 06:58am on Thursday morning local time. It was spotted near Cunicea, in the Camenca district, travelling from Ukraine towards Moldova, they said, but disappeared from radar at 7:11am. The airspace reopened as normal half an hour later. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/15/us-e.text: The US Treasury Department on Thursday extended a sanctions waiver for Russian oil giant Lukoil, allowing its service stations outside Russia to continue operating until April 2027.The extension allows Lukoil-branded petrol stations in countries including the United States to continue serving customers until 24 April 2027, replacing an earlier licence due to expire later this month.However, the latest licence maintains restrictions on the "transfer of funds to any person or account located in the Russian Federation".The decision comes a week after US President Donald Trump announced an agreement with Russia to supply diesel to US and global markets, prompting the Treasury to issue a temporary licence to facilitate deliveries.The deal, as announced by Trump on social media, envisages that Moscow will release 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global markets immediately, with an additional 500,000 tonnes in November and one million more after that.The Trump-Putin diesel deal has been badly received by EU foreign ministers, who say it undermines transatlantic unity at a time when Russia intensifies its attacks on Ukraine.Oil prices remain elevated as the war in the Middle East enters its eighth month, following a sharp rise in energy costs since the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran in late February.Tehran's retaliation included the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, a key passage for global oil transit, sending costs up.

https://www.thenationalnews.com/business.text: Energy market insiders who gathered in a vast underground ballroom in central London this week were united in support of a new emphasis on resilience in the oil industry. The duration of the US-Iran war has changed the industry from "a just-in-time to a just-in-case" sector, TotalEnergies chief executive Patrick Pouyanne told the Energy Intelligence Forum. Amin Nasser, chief executive of Aramco, said that throughout the crisis conditions, the producer has not cancelled one committed delivery, thanks to a number of routes to market and, in the case of the East-West pipeline, a vast capacity. This comes despite the supply problems caused by the blockades in the Strait of Hormuz and, more recently, the Bab Al Mandeb strait. “It [the pipeline] has multiple lines with a lot of redundancy and flexibility built in and, because of that, all our customers are getting all their shipments required,” he said. “When this crisis happened, we said, “OK, we have three routes. Is that enough?” Mr Nasser added. “Maybe not for the future. And this is the responsibility of the current generation, to think of a fourth and a fifth export way out.” Sheikh Nawaf Al Sabah, chief executive of Kuwait Petroleum Corporation (KPC), pointed out the value of having its own tanker fleet, which dates back to the 1990s. “I think there is a major difference that we are able to accomplish through our tankers by having these tankers owned by us,” Mr Al Sabah said. “We control where they go and the crews are our own crews. They, of course, all have the discretion of deciding whether they want to go through a passage or not.” An emerging picture of new codes of conduct from the US-Iran war stretches across customers, consuming nations, producers and product classes. Vaclav Bartuška, the Czech ambassador to the UK, said the long-term forces of change bear some resemblance to calculations last seen between the US and former Soviet Union. “We are relearning the escalation ladder, which was the basis of the Cold War for 40 years,” he told The National. “You know the level to which you escalate, that you deter, but also don't cause too much pain into the other side. “The Soviet Union and the United States developed a code, a language of how to hit each other without actually having open war between them. [They] managed to spend 40 years in a Cold War without killing the world. They had proxy wars. They had plenty of conflicts. They managed not to have a direct escalation among themselves. This could be a very long confrontation. It could also end the next day,” he said. During the gas dispute between Russia and Ukraine in January 2009, Mr Bartuska was involved in negotiations with Russian, Ukrainian and European Union leadership, when the Czech Republic held the EU Presidency. He also served as the Czech Republic's ambassador-at-large for energy security. Ichiro Takahara, chairman and chief executive of Japan's strategic reserves specialist operator, Jogmec, said diversification to avoid “chokepoints” was one priority in the country's stockpiling policy. He added that relations with resilient suppliers, such as Aramco and KPC, would include co-operation to build storage depots closer to customers in places such as Japan. Another Japanese executive, Takayuki Ueda, president of Inpex, said buyers now had wider considerations concerning diversification as well as resilience. “What matters for our buyers is security of supply,” he said. “They usually point out diversification of supply sources is important. However, they also emphasise the security and resilience of entire supply chain.” Countries with differing strengths must work together to boost supply undertakings, said Kevin Gallagher, managing director of Australian company Santos. “There's a real clarity and understanding with policymakers in Australia that more pragmatic rather than ideological policies when it comes to energy development and energy supply going forward is what was required,” he said. Mr Gallagher predicted Australia would “take its foot off the hose” that has restricted oil and gas exploration in recent years. The Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022 led European legislators to seek new energy deals in the Gulf – but the current war has narrowed those options. Mr Bartuška said European governments were likely to pursue a diversification of suppliers. “This is not a crisis yet. We have been through much worse, and European countries didn't start this conflict and are not taking direct part in it,” he said. Rising oil and gas prices would make some previously marginal projects more economically viable. “There are quite a few projects around the world which were basically on the threshold between being relevant and not,” Mr Bartuška said. “I think higher prices will make them sustainable economically. From Latin America, from African countries and projects in Asia, Australia or the US. There are quite a few resources which are not yet reserves, or they are becoming reserves, which means economically viable, thanks to the situation now.” “I think, in general, the European perception of war changed in 2022 with the start of the Russian war against Ukraine, and we now see huge attacks by drones and missiles very regularly,” he said. “There are also plenty of hybrid or hidden warfare and hidden attacks or deniable attacks against our installations. We are much more careful about what's happening in our countries, trying to deter another attack [while at] the same time, not to escalate too much.” He said western misconception of Iran was driving the inability to reach a truce – as well as a desire from the US and Iran sides to keep the war going. “I don't know if both sides actually want the end of confrontation. I'm not sure of that. It's been going on since the end of February. It's now October,” he said.
